reading_a.passage:
For years, organizations treated meetings as if their main cost were the time shown on the calendar. A one-hour meeting with eight people, managers reasoned, consumed eight staff-hours. That arithmetic is correct but incomplete. Meetings also break up periods of concentrated work, and the cost of interruption is not limited to the minutes spent switching tasks. After an interruption, people often need time to reconstruct what they were doing, recover relevant information, and regain the level of attention they had before.

This does not mean that meetings are inherently wasteful. Some problems genuinely benefit from real-time interaction. When a decision depends on disagreement, negotiation, or the rapid integration of information held by different people, a conversation can resolve uncertainty faster than a chain of messages. The mistake is to infer from these cases that synchronous discussion is the natural default for all coordination.

A number of firms have therefore tried to distinguish between work that needs simultaneity and work that merely needs visibility. Routine updates, status reports, and background explanations can often be recorded in a shared document. Participants can read them when they reach a natural break in their own work. Meetings can then be reserved for issues where the value comes from immediate response: a contested trade-off, an ambiguous problem, or a decision that cannot progress without several people reacting to one another.

The apparent efficiency of this approach, however, can be exaggerated. Written updates are not free. Poorly organized documents may take longer to read than a concise conversation, and asynchronous systems can encourage people to produce more information than anyone can use. The point is not that written communication is always superior. It is that the form of communication should match the coordination problem.

This distinction matters because attempts to improve productivity often focus on visible quantities: fewer meetings, shorter messages, smaller teams. But reducing a visible quantity does not automatically reduce the underlying coordination cost. A company can cut meeting hours and still make work harder if important disagreements are pushed into slow, fragmented exchanges. The better question is not “How can we eliminate meetings?” but “Which interactions require people to think together at the same time?”

reading_a.passage:
Public discussions of scientific uncertainty often assume that uncertainty is a temporary defect: once researchers collect enough data, it will disappear. In some fields that expectation is reasonable. A better measurement device can narrow the range of plausible values for a physical quantity, and a larger sample can make an estimate more precise. Yet many important scientific questions concern systems in which uncertainty cannot be reduced to zero because the future depends on interacting processes, human behavior, and events that are themselves difficult to predict.

Climate projections offer a useful example. Researchers can estimate how the atmosphere responds to greenhouse gases with increasing precision, but long-term outcomes also depend on future emissions, land use, technology, and policy. A model therefore may produce several scenarios rather than a single forecast. This is not equivalent to saying that “anything could happen.” The scenarios are constrained by physical knowledge and by explicit assumptions. Their spread represents a structured range of possibilities, not ignorance without boundaries.

Problems arise when this structure is lost in public communication. One common response is to suppress uncertainty for fear that audiences will interpret it as weakness. Another is to display every caveat without explaining which uncertainties matter for the decision at hand. Both approaches can mislead. False certainty hides genuine risk, while an undifferentiated list of uncertainties can make well-supported conclusions look fragile.

Decision makers rarely need uncertainty to vanish. They need to know whether different plausible futures would change the action they should take. If a bridge design is safe across a wide range of rainfall estimates, engineers do not need the exact rainfall fifty years from now. Conversely, if small changes in an estimate would alter the best decision, then uncertainty deserves more attention.

The practical challenge, then, is not simply to communicate “how uncertain” science is. It is to connect uncertainty to consequences. A range matters when it changes what should be done. This shifts the conversation from a demand for impossible certainty to a more useful question: which uncertainties are decision-relevant?

reading_a.passage:
Museums have traditionally been judged by what they preserve and display. Increasingly, however, they are also evaluated by what visitors do with what they encounter. This has encouraged many institutions to redesign exhibitions around participation: touchable replicas, interactive screens, open storage, workshops, and spaces where visitors can leave responses.

Participation can deepen attention, but only under certain conditions. An interactive feature earns its place when it helps visitors notice a relationship that would otherwise remain obscure, test an interpretation, or compare alternatives. By contrast, activity added merely to prevent boredom may fragment attention. Pressing a button is not automatically more educational than looking carefully at an object.

This distinction has implications for how museums use digital technology. Digital layers can reveal hidden information: the reverse side of a painting, changes made during restoration, or different reconstructions of an archaeological site. But screens can also compete with the original object. If visitors spend most of their time navigating an interface, the technology may become the exhibit rather than a means of seeing the exhibit more clearly.

Some museums respond by asking whether each interactive element changes the quality of observation. That question is deliberately narrower than “Is this engaging?” Engagement is valuable, but it is not a sufficient criterion. A dramatic display may attract attention without directing it toward anything worth learning; a quiet comparison may produce less excitement while supporting more careful judgment.

The broader lesson extends beyond museums. Designers often treat participation as an unquestioned good because it appears to give users agency. Yet more action does not necessarily mean more meaningful involvement. Participation is useful when the action is connected to a cognitive purpose. Otherwise, interaction can become a decorative layer that consumes attention without improving understanding.

reading_a.passage:
Organizations that want better decisions often invest in collecting more data. Yet the limiting factor is frequently not the amount of information available but the way evidence enters a decision process. A team may possess excellent data and still reach a poor conclusion if members search only for information that supports an early preference or if inconvenient evidence arrives too late to influence the choice.

One proposed remedy is to assign someone the formal role of critic. The critic's task is to challenge assumptions, identify missing evidence, and construct the strongest case against the favored option. Advocates argue that this can make dissent legitimate: questioning the emerging consensus becomes part of the job rather than a sign of disloyalty.

The method has limits. A designated critic may become predictable and therefore easy to ignore. Other members can treat disagreement as “the critic's responsibility” and stop testing their own assumptions. Moreover, if the same person repeatedly plays the role, the group may begin to discount that person's objections before hearing them.

Some teams therefore rotate the responsibility or use a different procedure: before the final decision, every member must state what evidence would cause them to change their mind. This shifts attention from defending positions to specifying conditions for revision. It also makes hidden asymmetries visible. A person who can name no possible disconfirming evidence may be protecting an identity or commitment rather than evaluating a hypothesis.

No procedure guarantees objectivity. The value of these methods is more modest. They alter the social and cognitive conditions under which contrary evidence can be heard. Better decisions do not arise simply because more information exists; they require structures that allow relevant information to change what people believe.

options: make disagreement socially legitimate within the group

options: the critic may gain excessive authority over data collection

options: who should act as the group's next critic
whether disagreement is caused by incomplete information
whether their positions are genuinely revisable

options: assigning formal roles to members with different opinions

part_b.directions: Choose the five paragraphs that best fill gaps 1–5. Two candidates are extra.
body: Cities often try to encourage walking by improving sidewalks, adding trees, or reducing traffic speed. These changes matter, but whether people actually walk also depends on what destinations exist within reach.

This helps explain why two neighborhoods with equally attractive streets can produce different walking patterns. In one, daily needs are scattered across long distances; in the other, shops, schools, and transit are close enough to combine errands on foot.

The same principle applies to public transport. A station can be clean and reliable, yet still attract few riders if reaching it requires crossing dangerous roads or walking through a disconnected street network.

This is why planners increasingly examine networks rather than isolated facilities. A sidewalk, crossing, bus stop, park, and shop can each work well individually but still fail as a system if the links among them are weak.
That perspective also changes how success is measured. Counting new sidewalks is useful, but the more important question is whether people can reach more of the places they value without a car.

candidates.A: In other words, the quality of the route cannot be separated from the usefulness of where the route leads.
candidates.B: For decades, transport policy focused mainly on the speed of private vehicles.
candidates.C: A short missing link can therefore matter more than a long stretch of already adequate infrastructure.
candidates.D: Walking is especially common among people who already exercise regularly.
candidates.E: Improving accessibility means looking not only at distance but at whether the entire trip can be completed safely and conveniently.
candidates.F: A network view does not imply that every street must serve every purpose equally.
candidates.G: The result is a shift from asking how much infrastructure exists to asking what opportunities that infrastructure actually connects.

body: Feedback is often described as information about past performance. Useful feedback, however, also changes what a learner does next.

A comment such as “be clearer” identifies a problem but does not necessarily reveal what should change. By contrast, pointing to an ambiguous claim and asking what evidence would make it precise gives the learner an actionable next step.

Timing matters as well. Immediate correction is valuable when an error would otherwise be repeated several times, but constant interruption can prevent learners from completing a thought or seeing the consequences of their own choices.

This suggests that effective feedback is not simply more frequent feedback. It is information delivered at a moment and level of detail that preserves the learner's responsibility for solving the problem.
The same idea explains why model answers can help or harm. Used after a genuine attempt, they provide a comparison. Shown too early, they can replace the learner's generation process.

candidates.A: The central question is therefore not whether feedback is positive or negative, but whether it changes the next decision in a useful way.
candidates.B: Students also differ greatly in how much praise they prefer to receive.
candidates.C: This distinction separates feedback that merely labels performance from feedback that supports revision.
candidates.D: For that reason, a pause before feedback can sometimes be part of good teaching rather than a delay in teaching.
candidates.E: The goal is not to remove difficulty but to place information where it improves independent control.
candidates.F: Written comments are usually remembered longer than spoken comments.
candidates.G: A good feedback system should therefore preserve a clear boundary between assistance and the learner's own first attempt.

paragraphs: Digital archives can make millions of documents searchable, but searchability changes how people explore a collection. Users often begin with a precise query rather than browsing neighboring materials, which can reduce accidental discovery.

Some archives respond by designing interfaces that restore a form of neighborhood. A user viewing one document may also see items created in the same place, period, or project, even when those items do not match the original search terms.

This does not mean that digital systems should imitate physical shelves. Digital collections can create relationships that shelves cannot, linking material by person, event, theme, or citation across distant locations.

The design challenge is therefore to balance directed retrieval with productive surprise. Too little structure leaves users lost; too much search precision can hide relevant material that the user did not know to request.

Evaluation should reflect this balance. Counting successful searches shows whether known targets are reachable, but archives should also ask whether users discover useful material beyond their initial query.
headings: A. Measuring discovery as well as retrieval
B. Why physical shelves remain superior
C. Recreating useful context around a found item
D. The hidden cost of precise search
E. Replacing search with recommendation systems
F. Balancing intentional search and unexpected discovery
G. Digital links can create new forms of context

paragraphs: When institutions publish performance targets, employees naturally adapt to them. This can improve focus, but it can also narrow attention toward what is measured.

A hospital judged only by waiting time may speed the first contact with patients while shifting delays to later stages that are not counted. The metric improves, yet the patient's total experience may not.
The problem is not measurement itself. Good metrics can reveal trends that intuition misses and make persistent failures difficult to ignore.
Trouble begins when a measure designed to inform judgment becomes a substitute for judgment. At that point, people optimize the number even when the number no longer tracks the underlying goal.
One safeguard is to pair a headline measure with checks on side effects and with periodic review of whether the metric still predicts what decision makers actually care about.

D. How a narrow target can improve one number while worsening the whole process
